items.q: Which box correctly represents NaCl dissolved in water?
options: W
X
Y
Z

items.q: What is wrong with box X?
options: Like partial charges face each other: water's δ+ H points at Na⁺ and its δ− O at Cl⁻.
It shows the ions separated, but in water the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions stay bonded together.
It has too many water molecules, because each ion attracts one water molecule.
It shows Cl⁻ as larger than Na⁺, but the chloride ion is the smaller of the two.

items.q: Why is box Y not a correct picture of the solution?
options: Dissolving separates the ions, and each ion is hydrated; Y shows an ion pair that has not come apart.
Y has too few water molecules in it to represent water as the solvent for the solution.
Y shows the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in a 1 : 1 ratio, but the ratio in the solution is 2 : 1.
Y shows covalent bonds inside the water molecules, which break when salt dissolves in water.

items.q: Box Z has the water oriented correctly. What error does it make?
options: It has a net charge of +1, because there are two Na⁺ for one Cl⁻ instead of a 1 : 1 ratio.
It shows the Na⁺ ions hydrated, but a cation is not surrounded by water molecules.
It spreads the ions through the box, but dissolved ions settle at the bottom of the box.
It shows Na⁺ and Cl⁻ separated, but NaCl dissolves as molecules, not as ions.

items.q: How many solute particles (ions) are shown in the box?

mistakes.why: Value: you counted each sulfur and oxygen atom separately. A sulfate ion is one particle; its covalent bonds do not break.

items.q: Why does the drawing show twice as many K⁺ ions as SO₄²⁻ ions?
options: K₂SO₄ gives two K⁺ for each SO₄²⁻, so the charges balance: 2(+1) + (−2) = 0.
K⁺ ions are smaller, so more of them fit into the same volume of the solution.
Half of the sulfate ions break apart into sulfur and oxygen atoms when dissolved.
Potassium ions attract more water, so more of them dissolve than sulfate ions.

items.q: Water molecules are added to the drawing around one K⁺ ion and one SO₄²⁻ ion. How should they point?
options: O toward K⁺; H toward the O atoms of SO₄²⁻.
H toward K⁺; O toward the O atoms of SO₄²⁻.
O toward both ions, because oxygen is the larger atom.
H toward both ions, because hydrogen bonds to both.

items.q: If the box represents 0.150 M K₂SO₄, what is the molarity of K⁺ ions?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the molarity of K₂SO₄ itself. Each formula unit releases two K⁺ ions.
Value: you halved it. There are twice as many K⁺ ions as formula units, so double.

items.q: Which ion attracts the water molecules around it most strongly?
options: K⁺ (radius 138 pm)
Na⁺ (radius 102 pm)
Ca²⁺ (radius 100 pm)
Mg²⁺ (radius 72 pm)

items.q: Which particle diagram describes an aqueous solution of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆?
options: Whole glucose molecules spread among water molecules
Separate C, H and O atoms spread among water molecules
Glucose⁺ and glucose⁻ ions surrounded by water
Glucose molecules piled in a layer at the bottom

items.q: A correct particle diagram of 0.10 M Ca(NO₃)₂(aq) shows which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: Two NO₃⁻ ions for every Ca²⁺ ion
Each NO₃⁻ ion drawn as one N bonded to three O
Ca²⁺ ions with water hydrogens pointing toward them
Separate N and O atoms from broken nitrate ions
Ions spread evenly through the box
Ca(NO₃)₂ units with the ions still touching

items.q: A student draws dissolved KBr with each water molecule's oxygen pointing toward BOTH the K⁺ and the Br⁻ ions, "because oxygen is the part of water that bonds." Which response is best?
options: Water orients by charge: δ− O faces K⁺, but δ+ H must face Br⁻, since O facing Br⁻ would repel.
The drawing is correct, because the oxygen atom forms hydrogen bonds with the ions in solution.
The drawing is correct for K⁺ and Br⁻ alike, because both are ions with a full charge on them.
Water should point H toward both ions, because H is the δ+ end and so it attracts ions.

items.q: Each box below represents equal volumes of 0.20 M solutions. Which solution has the most solute particles in the box?
options: 0.20 M sucrose
0.20 M NaCl
0.20 M MgSO₄
0.20 M AlCl₃

items.q: A box representing a solution of FeCl₃ shows 12 chloride ions. How many iron(III) ions should it show?

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied by 3. There are three Cl⁻ for each Fe³⁺, so divide.
Value: the ratio is not 1 : 1. FeCl₃ gives three Cl⁻ per Fe³⁺.

items.q: Solid KCl is added to water and stirred until it has all dissolved. Which change at the particle level allows the solution to conduct electricity?
options: The K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions separate and can move independently through the water.
The K–Cl covalent bonds break, releasing free electrons that carry the current.
Water molecules break into H⁺ and OH⁻ ions when they touch the KCl crystal.
The KCl units stay together but become polar, so they line up with the current.

items.q: What is the Rf of the drink's higher spot?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided the solvent distance by the spot distance. Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent distance, so it is never above 1.

items.q: Which dyes are present in the drink? Select all that apply.
options: Dye A
Dye B
Dye C
Dye D

items.q: Dye D has the smallest Rf. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Dye D is held most strongly by the paper relative to the solvent.
Dye D has the most mass, so it is too heavy to be carried far up the paper.
Dye D interacts most strongly with the solvent, so it stays near the start line.
Dye D was spotted last, so it had the least time to travel up the paper.

items.q: The student marked the start line in ink instead of pencil. How might this affect the results?
options: The ink could separate into its own spots and be mistaken for dyes in the drink.
The ink line would block the solvent from rising, so the spots would stay on the start line.
There is no effect, because the ink line is below the spots and is not part of the samples.
Each Rf would double, because the ink adds its own distance to each measured spot distance.

items.q: The experiment is repeated with a much less polar solvent. What would most likely happen to the Rf values of these polar food dyes?
options: They would decrease, because the dyes would be held more by the polar paper.
They would increase, because a less polar solvent moves faster up the paper and carries the dyes.
They would stay the same, because Rf depends on the dye and not on the solvent used.
They would rise to about 1.00, because the dyes would move with the solvent front.

items.q: Which liquid is collected first?
options: Water, which boils at about 100 °C
Acetone, which boils at about 56 °C
Both at once, in equal amounts
Neither, until 100 °C is reached

items.q: Which statement best explains why acetone distills first?
options: Acetone has weaker intermolecular forces, so its vapor pressure is higher.
Acetone molecules are heavier than water molecules, so they rise into the vapor first.
Water molecules break apart at 56 °C, so they stay behind in the boiling flask.
Acetone hydrogen-bonds more strongly than water, so it leaves the liquid together.

items.q: About how much acetone was in the original mixture?
options: About 10 mL
About 30 mL
About 60 mL
About 100 mL

items.q: The 35 mL sample, collected at 78 °C, is tested. What is it most likely to be?
options: A mixture of both, since 78 °C lies between their boiling points.
Pure acetone, since the liquid collected below 100 °C is acetone.
Pure water, since water starts to boil once the temperature passes 61 °C.
A new compound, formed when acetone and water reacted during heating.

items.q: Which method separates sand from a mixture of sand and salt water?
options: Filtration
Chromatography
Distillation
Evaporating the water

items.q: Why does filtration not separate the salt from salt water?
options: Dissolved ions are far smaller than the pores of the paper.
Salt ions stick to the filter paper and block it before any water passes.
Filtration works on gases, not on liquids such as salt water.
The salt reacts with the paper and forms a new dissolved compound.

items.q: Which method would best recover pure water from seawater?
options: Distillation, because water vaporizes while the ions stay behind.
Filtration, because the ions are trapped by the filter paper.
Chromatography, because the salt moves faster than the water.
Decanting, because the salt settles to the bottom over time.

items.q: Hexane (C₆H₁₄) and 1-propanol (C₃H₇OH) are separated on a column packed with polar silica (covered in –OH groups) using a nonpolar solvent. Which comes out of the column first, and why?
options: Hexane, because it is barely attracted to the polar silica.
1-Propanol, because it hydrogen-bonds to the solvent and is carried along.
Hexane, because it is the heavier molecule and falls through the column faster.
1-Propanol, because it has fewer carbon atoms and fits through the packing.

items.q: On a chromatogram, the solvent front is 12.5 cm from the start line and a spot is 4.0 cm from it. What is the spot's Rf?

mistakes.why: Value: you inverted the ratio. Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent distance, which is at most 1.

items.q: Which differences in physical properties are used to separate mixtures? Select all that apply.
options: Particle size (filtration)
Attraction to a stationary phase (chromatography)
Vapor pressure (distillation)
Number of protons in the nucleus
Molar mass alone (heavier parts left behind)
Total mass of the sample

items.q: Put the steps for running a paper chromatogram in order.
options: Draw a pencil start line near the bottom of the paper
Place a small spot of each sample on the line
Stand the paper in solvent below the start line
Remove the paper when the solvent is near the top and mark the solvent front
Measure the distances and calculate each Rf

items.q: Which statement describes the trend in the graph?
options: Solubility in water falls as the carbon chain gets longer.
Solubility in water rises as the carbon chain gets longer.
Solubility in water is about the same for each alcohol.
Solubility rises to a maximum at 6 carbons, then falls.

items.q: Which explanation accounts for the trend?
options: A longer nonpolar chain costs more water–water hydrogen bonds; the one –OH adds the same.
Longer alcohols have more –OH groups, which repel the water molecules around them.
Longer alcohols are heavier, and heavier molecules sink rather than dissolving.
Longer chains are more polar, so they are attracted to water too strongly to dissolve.

items.q: Based on the trend, how would 1-octanol (8 carbons) dissolve in water?
options: It would be miscible with water
About 7.7 g per 100 g water
Between 0.17 and 0.59 g per 100 g water
Less than 0.17 g per 100 g water

items.q: 1-Hexanol dissolves only slightly in water, but it mixes completely with hexane (C₆H₁₄). Which explanation is best?
options: Its chain attracts hexane by dispersion forces like those hexane loses; in water it costs hydrogen bonds.
Hexane hydrogen-bonds to the –OH group of 1-hexanol more strongly than water can.
1-Hexanol becomes nonpolar when mixed with hexane, because its –OH group breaks off.
Hexane molecules repel water, so they push 1-hexanol out of the water and into the hexane.

items.q: How does the solubility of O₂ in water change as the temperature rises?
options: It increases.
It decreases.
It stays the same.
It increases, then decreases.

items.q: Which particle-level explanation accounts for the trend?
options: Faster dissolved O₂ molecules escape their weak attractions to water more easily.
At higher temperature, water molecules hydrogen-bond more strongly to O₂ and pull it apart into atoms.
At higher temperature, O₂ molecules become polar and are repelled by the polar water molecules.
At higher temperature, the air contains less oxygen, so less of it can dissolve in the water.

items.q: A power plant releases warm water into a river. Which consequence follows from the data?
options: The warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen, which can stress fish.
The warmer water holds more dissolved oxygen, which helps fish.
The dissolved oxygen is unchanged, because the air above is unchanged.
The dissolved oxygen is driven out at once at 40 °C.

items.q: At 20 °C, how would the dissolved O₂ change if the water were in contact with pure O₂ at 1.00 atm instead of air?
options: It would increase, because a higher O₂ pressure drives more O₂ in.
It would decrease, because pure O₂ pushes on the water and squeezes the dissolved gas out.
It would stay at 9.1 mg/L, because the solubility of O₂ is set by temperature.
It would fall to zero, because pure O₂ would react with the water to form a new compound.

items.q: Which substance is most likely to dissolve well in hexane, C₆H₁₄?
options: Iodine, I₂
Sodium chloride, NaCl
Sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁
Methanol, CH₃OH

items.q: Why does ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, mix with water in all proportions?
options: Its –OH group hydrogen-bonds to water and its chain is short.
It is an ionic compound that separates into ions surrounded by water molecules.
It has the same molar mass as water, so the two liquids have equal densities.
Its molecules are nonpolar, so they fit between water molecules without any attraction.

items.q: A student says, "Oil and water separate because oil molecules and water molecules repel each other." Which is the best correction?
options: They attract weakly; water molecules attract each other much more.
They attract strongly, but oil molecules are too large to fit into the spaces between water molecules.
They repel because both are polar, and like charges on polar molecules push each other away.
They separate because oil is denser than water and sinks below it, which keeps the layers apart.

items.q: Which pairs of liquids are likely to mix completely? Select all that apply.
options: Water and methanol, CH₃OH
Hexane and octane, C₈H₁₈
Water and hexane
Water and carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄

items.q: A sealed bottle of soda is at 5 °C under CO₂ at 3.5 atm. Predict how the amount of CO₂ dissolved changes after each change.

variables.name: The bottle is opened, so the CO₂ pressure above the soda falls to about 0.0004 atm
The sealed bottle is gently turned upside down and back at 5 °C

items.q: What does "like dissolves like" mean?
options: Substances with similar kinds of intermolecular forces tend to dissolve in each other.
Substances with similar molar masses tend to dissolve in each other.
Substances of the same color tend to dissolve in each other.
Substances in the same state of matter tend to dissolve in each other.

items.q: Vitamin C has several –OH groups; vitamin A is mostly a long carbon–hydrogen chain with one –OH. Which statement is best supported?
options: Vitamin C dissolves well in water; vitamin A dissolves better in oils.
Vitamin A dissolves well in water; vitamin C dissolves better in fats and oils.
Both dissolve equally well in water, because each has at least one –OH group.
Neither dissolves in water, because both are molecular compounds.

items.q: What happens in the molecules when they absorb the light at about 3,350 cm⁻¹?
options: An O–H bond vibrates more strongly.
An electron moves to a higher energy level.
The molecule rotates faster.
An inner electron is removed.

items.q: Which compound is the unknown most likely to be?
options: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH
Acetone, (CH₃)₂C=O
Hexane, C₆H₁₄
Water, H₂O

items.q: The O–H absorption is at a higher wavenumber than the C–O absorption. What does this tell you?
options: Exciting the O–H vibration needs a higher-energy photon than exciting the C–O vibration.
The O–H bond absorbs more light than the C–O bond, because the dip is deeper.
The O–H bond vibrates more slowly than the C–O bond, because it is a lighter bond.
The O–H absorption moves an electron, while the C–O absorption moves the whole molecule.

items.q: A sample of acetone is run on the same instrument. Which change would you expect in its spectrum compared with the unknown?
options: A new strong dip near 1,700 cm⁻¹ and no broad dip near 3,350 cm⁻¹.
The same spectrum, because both liquids contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
No dips, because acetone is a polar molecule and so it does not absorb infrared.
A dip in the visible region, because acetone is a colored liquid.

items.q: At which wavelength does the dye absorb most strongly?
options: About 450 nm
About 540 nm
About 630 nm
About 700 nm

items.q: What color does the dye solution appear?
options: Blue, because it absorbs red-orange light.
Red, because it absorbs red light most strongly.
Black, because it absorbs light across the visible spectrum.
Colorless, because it absorbs just one narrow band.

items.q: What happens to a dye molecule when it absorbs a 630 nm photon?
options: An electron moves from a lower energy level to a higher one.
A bond in the molecule vibrates with more energy.
The molecule rotates faster about its center.
A covalent bond breaks and the molecule falls apart.

items.q: Would shining 1,500 nm light on the dye cause the same electronic transition? Why?
options: No: a 1,500 nm photon carries less energy than the gap.
Yes: a longer wavelength carries more energy, which is more than enough for the gap.
Yes: any photon is absorbed once the light is bright enough, whatever its wavelength.
No: 1,500 nm light is an X-ray, which removes inner electrons instead.

items.q: Put these regions in order of increasing energy per photon.
options: Radio waves
Microwaves
Infrared
Visible light
Ultraviolet
X-rays

items.q: Which pairings of a type of radiation with the change it causes in a molecule are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Microwave: faster rotation
Infrared: more bond vibration
Ultraviolet: faster rotation
Visible: more bond vibration
Ultraviolet: electrons promoted to higher levels
Radio: inner electrons removed

items.q: Why does a microwave oven heat water but leave a dry glass plate fairly cool?
options: Microwaves make polar water molecules rotate faster, warming the food.
Microwaves carry more energy per photon than visible light, so they break the bonds in water.
Microwaves promote electrons in water to excited states, which give off heat as they return.
Microwaves make the glass vibrate, and the glass passes the heat to the water molecules in the food.

items.q: Which kind of radiation has the longest wavelength?
options: Ultraviolet
Visible
Infrared
Microwave

items.q: Ultraviolet light can damage skin cells, but infrared light from a heat lamp of the same brightness does not. Which explanation fits?
options: Each UV photon carries enough energy to excite electrons; an IR photon does not.
UV light is hotter than IR light, so it raises the skin's temperature more quickly.
IR light is absorbed by air before it reaches the skin, so very little arrives.
UV light has a longer wavelength, so it reaches deeper into the skin's cells.

items.q: Nitrogen, N₂, makes up 78% of the air but is not a greenhouse gas, while CO₂ absorbs infrared strongly. Which claim is consistent with this?
options: N₂'s vibration does not absorb infrared; CO₂ has vibrations that do.
N₂ absorbs infrared more strongly than CO₂ but is too common to matter.
N₂ absorbs ultraviolet light, so it holds the most heat in the atmosphere.
CO₂ absorbs infrared because its electrons jump to higher energy levels.

items.q: A molecule's two lowest electronic levels are far apart, but its vibrational levels are close together. Which light could it absorb to excite a vibration but not an electronic transition?
options: X-ray
Ultraviolet
Visible
Infrared

items.q: What is the frequency of line A?

mistakes.why: Value: you used the wavelength in nm. Convert to meters first: 656.3 nm = 6.563 × 10⁻⁷ m.
Value: you divided λ by c. Frequency is ν = c/λ.

items.q: What is the energy of one photon of line A?
Which line comes from the largest drop in energy between two levels?
Why does hydrogen emit only these particular wavelengths rather than a continuous rainbow?
options: Its electron energies are quantized, so only photons matching the gaps between levels are emitted.
Its electrons can sit at any energy, but the spectroscope filters out the other wavelengths.
Hydrogen atoms are too small to emit light of any other color than these four.
Hot hydrogen gas reflects these four colors from the light in the room.

items.q: What is the energy of one mole of line D photons, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: that is one photon. Multiply by Avogadro's number for a mole of photons.

items.q: Which relationship does the graph show?
options: Energy per photon is inversely proportional to wavelength.
Energy per photon is directly proportional to wavelength.
Energy per photon falls by the same amount for each 100 nm.
Energy per photon does not depend on wavelength.

items.q: By what factor is the energy of a 250 nm photon greater than that of a 750 nm photon?

mistakes.why: Value: you inverted the ratio. The shorter wavelength has the greater energy.
Value: E depends on 1/λ, not 1/λ².

items.q: An electronic transition in a molecule requires 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Which wavelength of light could cause it?
options: About 200 nm
About 400 nm
About 600 nm
About 800 nm

items.q: A student says that a very bright red lamp (700 nm) can cause the transition in the previous question if it is bright enough. Which response is best?
options: No: each red photon has about 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, less than the gap, and brighter light only adds more such photons.
Yes: a brighter lamp has more energy in total, so it is able to supply the 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J needed.
Yes: bright light has a shorter wavelength than dim light, so it carries more energy per photon.
No: red light has more energy per photon than the gap, so it passes through without being absorbed.

items.q: A microwave oven uses radiation with a frequency of 2.45 × 10⁹ s⁻¹. What is its wavelength, in meters?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided ν by c. Wavelength is λ = c/ν.
Value: you multiplied c by ν. Wavelength is λ = c/ν.

items.q: Sodium street lamps emit yellow light at 589 nm. What is the energy of one photon of this light?
What is the energy of one mole of 589 nm photons, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Units: that is J/mol. Divide by 1000 to give kJ/mol.
Value: you used 589 nm as if it were meters. Convert: 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m.

items.q: Which equation gives the energy of one photon from its frequency?
options: E = hν
E = hλ
E = mc²
c = λν

items.q: When the wavelength of light is doubled, what happens to its frequency and to the energy of each photon?
options: Both are halved.
Both are doubled.
Frequency halves; energy doubles.
Frequency doubles; energy halves.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the energy of one mole of photons from a wavelength in nm in order.
options: Convert the wavelength from nm to m
Calculate the frequency, ν = c/λ
Calculate the energy of one photon, E = hν
Multiply by Avogadro's number to get J/mol
Convert J/mol to kJ/mol

items.q: An atom has two levels 3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ J apart. Which photons could it absorb to move an electron between exactly these two levels? Select all that apply.
options: 656 nm
486 nm
328 nm

items.q: Use the calibration curve to find the dye concentration in the diluted drink, in units of 10⁻⁵ M (for example, 3.00 means 3.00 × 10⁻⁵ M).

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied the absorbance by the slope. Concentration is A ÷ slope.

items.q: The slope of the line equals εb. With b = 1.00 cm, what is the molar absorptivity of the dye?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided concentration by absorbance. The slope is ΔA ÷ Δc.

items.q: Before measuring the drink, the student touches the clear faces of its cuvette, leaving fingerprints. How does this affect the concentration she reports?
options: Too high, because the fingerprints absorb or scatter light and raise the absorbance.
Too low, because the fingerprints let more light reach the detector.

items.q: Why does a colorless solution of sugar give an absorbance near zero at 630 nm?
